sections.h2: How Nebraska treats a quitclaim deed
sections.html:
A quitclaim deed is an ordinary deed for recording and tax purposes in Nebraska. One rule sets it apart: if the grantor later picks up more title, that extra title does not pass to the person who took the quitclaim. The rule is in Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-209.

The statute starts from the opposite position. When a deed claims to convey more than the grantor owned, anything the grantor acquires afterward normally flows to the grantee. Quitclaim and special warranty deeds are carved out of that benefit. The Nebraska court said the same in Troxell v. Stevens (1899).

The word deed is defined broadly. Under 76-203 it covers every written instrument that creates, transfers, mortgages or assigns real estate or an interest in it, other than wills and leases of one year or less. A quitclaim fits that definition, so the usual recording and transfer statement rules apply. The state's Form 521 even has its own box for "Quit Claim", next to warranty, corrective, sheriff and transfer on death.

sections.h2: What the register of deeds needs before recording
sections.html:
The register of deeds will record a quitclaim only if it is signed and acknowledged, follows the page format rules, and arrives with a completed Form 521. Each requirement lives in a different statute, which is why people miss one.

  • Acknowledgment. Inside Nebraska, 76-217 requires the acknowledgment to be made before a judge or clerk of any court, a United States magistrate, or a notary public. An officer cannot take an acknowledgment outside his or her territorial jurisdiction.
  • Blank space. 23-1503.01 calls for a blank area at the top of the first page, at least three inches by eight and one-half inches, for the recording stamp. Without it the office may add a page and charge for it.
  • Paper and print. Pages run between 8.5 by 11 and 8.5 by 14 inches, black text on white paper of at least twenty-pound weight. A font of at least eight points is presumed legible.
  • Signatures. Use black or dark blue ink; digital or electronic signatures are allowed. Type, print or stamp each party's name under the signature.
  • Transfer statement. Under 76-214, the grantee files a completed statement when the deed is presented. Without it the register shall not record the deed.

That statement is Form 521. The deed will not be recorded unless items 1 through 27 are filled in and the grantee or an authorized representative has signed.

Recording costs $10 for the first page and $6 for each added page, under 33-109. Of that, $2.50 of the first-page fee and 50 cents of each added page go toward preserving records and modernizing the register's office. A certified copy of a recorded instrument costs $1.50 per page.

The documentary stamp tax comes on top unless an exemption applies. The current rate is $3.32 for each $1,000 of value or fraction of a thousand, as shown on the Department of Revenue's stamp tax page. Section 76-901 drops the rate to $2.32 for transfers on or after January 1, 2032.

For a family quitclaim with no stated price, call the register of deeds in your county and ask whether the office applies market value or assessed value before you bring a check. Counties describe nominal-consideration transfers in different words.

sections.h2: Quitclaim deeds that skip the stamp tax
sections.html:
A quitclaim is exempt when it falls into a category in 76-902. For a house, the usual one is a transfer inside the family with no real consideration: between spouses, between ex-spouses for property acquired or held during the marriage, or between parent and child.

Other exemptions that often apply:

  • Deeds that confirm, correct, modify or supplement a recorded deed without extending or limiting the existing interest.
  • Deeds that secure or release a debt.
  • Deeds into a trust, when the same transfer would be exempt if made straight to the beneficiaries. The register must be shown a signed statement saying so, and the signer keeps the supporting evidence for inspection by the Department of Revenue.
  • Deeds from a trustee to a trust beneficiary.
  • Deeds of distribution by a personal representative to heirs or devisees.
  • Deeds to a qualifying 501(c)(3) nonprofit, without actual consideration.

The statute also presumes that a deed transferring legal title or a beneficial interest is taxable unless the face of the deed or documentary proof shows an exemption. Form 521 has a line for the exemption number, so cite the right one when you file.

sections.h2: What a quitclaim deed cannot do
sections.html:
A quitclaim moves whatever title the grantor holds. It does not repair a clouded title. Three limits come up often.

First, the after-acquired title rule above. If the grantor owned half and later inherits the other half, the quitclaim holder does not automatically get it.

Second, recording priority. Under 76-238, a recorded instrument takes effect against creditors and later good-faith purchasers from the moment it is delivered to the register. An unrecorded one is void against a later buyer without notice who records first, though it stays valid between the two parties. In Schott v. Dosh (1896), a quitclaim holder was allowed to be a bona fide purchaser, so the deed type alone does not block that protection.

Third, timing. Section 76-237 treats a deed as recorded from the moment it is delivered to the register, in the order delivered. A deed signed in October but filed in spring leaves a gap in which a later recorded deed can win.

A quitclaim does not wipe out a mortgage, a judgment lien or a tax lien. If the house carries any of those, a title search shows what the grantee really receives.

sections.h2: Selling a house you received by quitclaim
sections.html:
A house that arrived by quitclaim deed sells like any other, but the buyer's title company will read the deed closely. Expect questions about whether an authorized officer took the acknowledgment, whether Form 521 was filed with the right exemption cited, and whether the grantor held full title to begin with.

The usual stories are a parent adding a child to title, a divorce moving a house to one spouse, or an heir signing over a share. All are legitimate. Trouble starts when the paperwork was informal and never recorded, or when a co-owner's signature is missing.

  • Pull the recorded deed from the county register of deeds and confirm the recording date and the book and page.
  • Check that every person who held title signed the deed.
  • Confirm whether any mortgage or judgment against the former owner is still of record.
  • Keep a copy of the filed Form 521 and any exemption statement.

Our team buys Nebraska houses as-is, including homes with messy paper trails. Title work decides how fast a sale closes, so the sooner you can show the recorded deed, the sooner we can talk through the numbers.

faqs.q: Can I use a quitclaim deed to add someone to my Nebraska house title?
faqs.a: Yes. A quitclaim is a recordable deed under the definition in 76-203, so it can add a name. It needs an acknowledgment before an authorized officer, the proper page format and a Form 521 at the register of deeds. A deed to a spouse or child with no real consideration is on the stamp tax exemption list in 76-902.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to file a quitclaim deed in Nebraska?
faqs.a: The register of deeds charges $10 for the first page and $6 for each extra page under 33-109. A taxable deed also owes documentary stamp tax at $3.32 per $1,000 of value. Family transfers without consideration are exempt under 76-902.

faqs.q: Does the register of deeds check that a quitclaim deed is legally valid?
faqs.a: The register checks format and the transfer statement, not the underlying title. Under 76-214 the deed will not be recorded without a completed, signed Form 521, and the layout rules in 23-1503.01 apply. Whether the grantor really owned the property is a title question.

faqs.q: What happens if I never record my Nebraska quitclaim deed?
faqs.a: The deed stays valid between you and the person who signed it. Under 76-238, though, it is void against later good-faith purchasers and creditors who record first without notice. Recording promptly closes that gap.

faqs.q: Do I need a lawyer to prepare a Nebraska quitclaim deed?
faqs.a: The statutes do not require one, but the acknowledgment, format and tax rules are strict enough that mistakes are common. For anything beyond a simple, debt-free family transfer, ask a Nebraska real estate attorney or a title company to review it.
